title: Digital Design Lab
text:
Preface
Every processor, controller, and screen you have ever used began as a handful of logic gates someone arranged on purpose. This book is about learning to do that arranging yourself — not by reading about it, but by designing, simulating, and running your own digital circuits on real hardware.
Over nine labs, you will go from your first combinational circuit to a complete FPGA-based System on Chip: a HIPV, a Risc-V based processor, talking to peripherals you wrote, over a bus you configured, validated with a real oscilloscope. Along the way you will hit the same problems every digital designer hits — a signal that glitches, a counter that free-runs, a testbench that lies to you — and learn to reason your way out of them.
That debugging instinct, more than any single lab, is the point.
Note to Students: These notes are intended solely for educational purposes. They are not a replacement for attending lectures or consulting textbooks, but rather a complementary resource to support your learning.

title: 1  First exercise: Tools and the Digital Design Cycle
text:
1.1 The digital design cycle
This first lab has two goals. First, to introduce the digital design cycle — the sequence of steps every digital circuit goes through, from an idea to a working bitstream on real hardware — so that you understand why each later lab does what it does. Second, to get your machine set up with the toolchain we use throughout the course, so the remaining labs are about designing hardware rather than fighting installers.
Every design in this course, however small, passes through the same stages:
Steps 3–7 are exactly what a toolchain automates for you. Knowing this sequence matters because when something goes wrong, the first useful question is which stage failed — a syntax error is a design-entry problem, a mismatch with the testbench is a verification problem, an unroutable design is a place & route problem, and an LED that doesn’t light despite a clean build is a hardware/pin-constraint problem. Each points you to a different fix.
crumbs: 1  First exercise: Tools and the Digital Design Cycle

title: 1  First exercise: Tools and the Digital Design Cycle
text:
Specification — describe, in plain language, what the circuit must do: its inputs, its outputs, and the relationship between them.
RTL design entry — write that behavior in a hardware description language. In this course, that language is SystemVerilog.
Functional verification (simulation) — before touching real hardware, simulate the design against a testbench to check it behaves as specified. Bugs are far cheaper to find here than on a board.
Synthesis — translate the RTL description into a gate-level netlist: a graph of primitive logic cells and the wires connecting them.
Place & route (implementation) — map that netlist onto the FPGA’s actual resources (logic cells, routing wires, I/O pins), respecting the timing and pin constraints you provide.
Bitstream generation — package the placed-and-routed design into the binary configuration file the FPGA fabric loads on power-up.
Programming — load the bitstream onto the physical board.
Hardware validation — check that the programmed board actually does what you specified in step 1. If it doesn’t, you go back to step 1 or 2 and iterate.

title: 1  First exercise: Tools and the Digital Design Cycle
text:
1.2 Tools used in this course
In previous years this course used Xilinx Vivado, a proprietary, vendor-specific design suite. Starting this year, we use Anvil — a small, open-source CLI that drives an entirely open FPGA flow (no license, no account, no multi-GB installer). Anvil orchestrates the same stages described above using open tools:



Design cycle stage
Tool




Design entry
SystemVerilog (you write top.sv)


Simulation
Icarus Verilog (iverilog) + GTKWave, via anvil test


Synthesis
sv2v (SystemVerilog → Verilog) feeding Yosys


Place & route
VPR (part of the F4PGA project — Yosys + VPR together)


Bitstream generation
F4PGA


Programming
openFPGALoader



Anvil itself just wires these tools together behind a handful of commands (anvil init, anvil build, anvil test, anvil program) so you don’t invoke each one by hand.
Anvil supports two FPGA boards, the Digilent Nexys A7 100T and the Nexys A7 50T. Both boards are used across the exercises in this course.






NoteNexys A7 50T



Anvil supports both the Nexys A7 100T and the Nexys A7 50T (support for the 50T was added in Anvil 1.1.0).
Your own computer: a normal installation works out of the box. If you installed Anvil before the 50T was added, run anvil update once.
Classroom computers: these have an older Anvil and you cannot run anvil update there (it needs sudo). Apply the classroom patch instead; it needs no administrator rights and changes only files in your home directory:
wget https://gist.githubusercontent.com/RatkoFri/d12d34610a58260a58a803eec74e7185/raw/anvil-nexys50t.sh
bash anvil-nexys50t.sh
source ~/.bashrc
Run it once per account; running it again does no harm. Check the result with anvil boards (both boards should be listed) and anvil doctor. Then start a 50T project with:
anvil init --board Nexys-A7-50T --example switches-leds

title: 1  First exercise: Tools and the Digital Design Cycle
text:
1.3 Installing Anvil
Prerequisites: a native Ubuntu 22.04 LTS machine, or WSL2 on Windows (the docs call out the handful of WSL-only steps, mainly around forwarding the board’s USB connection, as “WSL only”). Docker support is not available yet.
The recommended path is the automated setup script:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LogiSmith/toolchain-setup/main/install.sh | bash
If you’d rather review the script before running it (always a reasonable instinct when piping a script into a shell):
git clone https://github.com/LogiSmith/toolchain-setup.git
cd toolchain-setup
less install.sh
./install.sh
A successful run ends with a green ✓ Toolchain installed and all tests passed banner. Open a new shell afterward (so your updated PATH/aliases take effect) and verify with:
anvil doctor
For manual, tool-by-tool installation steps, WSL2-specific USB forwarding, and troubleshooting, see the full LogiSmith installation docs — that page is the canonical reference and is more likely to stay current than a copy pasted here.






TipEditor tip: SystemVerilog syntax highlighting and linting in VS Code



Plain .sv files have no syntax highlighting in VS Code out of the box. Install Verilog-HDL/SystemVerilog (publisher mshr-h) for SystemVerilog syntax highlighting and snippets, plus linting that reports syntax and elaboration errors directly in the editor as you type, instead of only after running anvil build or iverilog.
The extension needs to be pointed at a linter. Since this course already installs Icarus Verilog as part of the Anvil toolchain, set verilog.linting.linter to iverilog in the extension’s settings rather than installing a separate tool like Verilator or Verible just for this. The iverilog executable needs to be on your PATH, which the Anvil installer already takes care of.

title: 1  First exercise: Tools and the Digital Design Cycle
text:
1.4 Your first design: basic_comb
With anvil doctor passing, build a first design that exercises switches and LEDs directly, with no clock involved: a small combinational circuit.
mkdir basic_comb && cd basic_comb
anvil init --board Nexys-A7-100T
This scaffolds a project:
basic_comb/
├── config.json    # board + module configuration
├── top.sv         # top-level design — edit this
├── *.xdc          # pin constraints, copied from the board master
├── tb/            # testbenches
└── Makefile

1.4.0.1 What’s in config.json
config.json is the per-project manifest every anvil command reads (build, test, program). anvil init --board Nexys-A7-100T fills it in for you, so you won’t normally hand-edit it in this lab — but it’s worth knowing what’s there:
{
  "project": "basic_comb",
  "board": "Nexys-A7-100T",
  "top": "top",
  "target": "nexys4ddr",
  "partname": "xc7a100tcsg324-1",
  "device": "artix7",
  "ofl_board": "nexys_a7_100",
  "xdc": "Nexys-A7-100T-Master.xdc"
}

project — the project’s name, defaulting to the directory name.
board — which entry of Anvil’s board registry (boards.json) this project targets; everything below top is copied in from that registry at anvil init time.
top — the top-level module name Anvil looks for when it builds your design. It defaults to top, which is exactly why the module in top.sv needs to be named top rather than basic_comb.
partname, device, target, ofl_board, xdc — board-specific details (exact FPGA part, device family, Makefile build target, openFPGALoader board identifier, and master constraints filename) that synthesis, place & route, and programming each need. You won’t touch these directly for the Nexys A7 100T.
modules (not shown above, since this design has none) — a list of reusable RTL module dependencies with pinned versions, e.g. "uart@1.0.0", added automatically by anvil addmodule. You’ll meet this once a later lab pulls in a shared peripheral block.

Replace the contents of top.sv with three switch inputs feeding four LED outputs through simple boolean logic. Anvil expects the top-level module in top.sv to be named top, so the logic below is the same as the basic_comb.sv starter file, just renamed from basic_comb to top:
// basic_comb — simple 3-input combinational logic
module top (
    input  logic a,        // SW0
    input  logic b,        // SW1
    input  logic c,        // SW2
    output logic [3:0] y   // LED0–LED3
);
    assign y[0] = a & b | c;
    assign y[1] = a & c;
    assign y[2] = a | c;
    assign y[3] = a & b & c;
endmodule


1.4.0.2 Explanation

Continuous assignment: each assign statement drives its output from a boolean expression of the inputs, re-evaluated any time a, b, or c changes. There is no clock and no memory — the outputs are a pure function of the current switch positions, which is exactly what “combinational logic” means.
This is the design-entry stage: assign is the idiomatic way to describe combinational logic in SystemVerilog, the same way always_ff (which you’ll meet in the next lab) is the idiom for sequential logic.
Four independent outputs: y[0]–y[3] are four separate circuits sharing the same three inputs — nothing requires a module to have only one output bit.

Uncomment (or check) the pins for a, b, c, and y in the generated .xdc file — they should look like this:
set_property PACKAGE_PIN J15 [get_ports {a}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {a}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN L16 [get_ports {b}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {b}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN M13 [get_ports {c}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {c}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN H17 [get_ports {y[0]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {y[0]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN K15 [get_ports {y[1]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {y[1]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN J13 [get_ports {y[2]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {y[2]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN N14 [get_ports {y[3]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {y[3]}]
This maps a, b, c to switches SW0–SW2 and y[0]–y[3] to LED0–LED3 on the Nexys A7 100T. Unlike Blinky, there’s no create_clock line here — a purely combinational design has no clock port for the timing analyzer to check.
Then build and program the board:
anvil build       # sv2v → Yosys → VPR → bitstream, a few seconds
anvil program     # flash the bitstream to the board via openFPGALoader
If everything worked, flipping SW0–SW2 should change the LED0–LED3 pattern according to the four equations above.

1.6 Assignment

Run anvil doctor and confirm every check passes. If something fails, consult the troubleshooting guide before asking for help.
Build and program the basic_comb design above, and confirm the LED pattern matches the equations for every switch combination.

title: 2  Second exercise: Introduction to (System)Verilog
text:
2.1 Types
Commonly used types in SystemVerilog include:

title: 2  Second exercise: Introduction to (System)Verilog
text:
2.1.1 Logic (NetList) Types

logic: A 4-state data type (0, 1, X, Z) used for modeling combinational and sequential logic.
bit: A 2-state data type (0, 1) used for modeling binary data.



2.1.2 Vector Types

bit [n-1:0]: An n-bit unsigned integer.
logic [n-1:0]: An n-bit unsigned integer with 4-state logic.



2.1.3 Variable Types

logic: A 4-state data type (0, 1, X, Z) used for modeling combinational and sequential logic.
byte: An 8-bit signed integer.
shortint: A 16-bit signed integer.
int: A 32-bit signed integer.
longint: A 64-bit signed integer.
integer: A general-purpose 32-bit signed integer (legacy from Verilog).
real: A 64-bit floating point variable.



2.1.4 Expressing Numbers Using Different Bases
// Binary representation (base 2)
logic [3:0] binary_num = 4'b1010; // 4-bit binary number 1010 (decimal 10)

// Octal representation (base 8)
logic [5:0] octal_num = 6'o12; // 6-bit octal number 12 (decimal 10)

// Decimal representation (base 10)
logic [7:0] decimal_num = 8'd10; // 8-bit decimal number 10

// Hexadecimal representation (base 16)
logic [7:0] hex_num = 8'hA; // 8-bit hexadecimal number A (decimal 10)

title: 2  Second exercise: Introduction to (System)Verilog
text:
2.2 Module
All system modules in Verilog are encapsulated inside a module. Modules can include instantiation of lower-level modules to support hierarchical designs. The keywords module and endmodule mark the beginning and the end of the system description.
module ModuleName(
    portType signalType Port1_name,
    portType signalType Port2_name, Port3_name,
    .......
    portType signalType PortN_name
);
where the portType specifies the direction of the port (input, output, or inout), and signalType defines the type of the signal, as described in the previous section.







Port Type
Description




input
Specifies an input port to the module. Data flows into the module through this port.


output
Specifies an output port from the module. Data flows out of the module through this port.


inout
Specifies a bidirectional port. Data can flow both into and out of the module through this port.

title: 2  Second exercise: Introduction to (System)Verilog
2  Second exercise: Introduction to (System)Verilog
text:
2.4 Modeling Concurent functionality in SystemVerilog

2.4.1 Continuous assignment
Continuous assignment in SystemVerilog allows for the assignment of values to nets using the assign keyword, ensuring that the assigned value is continuously updated whenever the right-hand side expression changes. A continuous assignment models combinational logic. For example:
assign out = a & b; // 'out' is continuously assigned the result of 'a & b'
We need to differ continous assignment from assignment in programming languages.
First example:
assign b = a; 
assign c = b;
In programming languages, a similar construct will first assign the value of a to b, and then pass the value of b to c. During synthesis, the tool will remove signal b and infer assign c = a.
Second example:
assign c = a; 
assign c = b;
In programming languages, a similar construct will first assign the value of a to c, and then assign the value of b to c. The final value of c will be determined by the last assignment. During synthesis, the tool will create a net driven by two signals. As these signals by have different values, the net c will have an unknown value X. This situation must be avoided at all costs.


2.4.2 4-bit 4:1 Multiplexer
The 4-bit multiplexer (MUX) selects one of the four 4-bit inputs to pass to the output based on the 2-bit selection signal.
module mux4to1 (
    input logic [3:0] in0, // 4-bit input 0
    input logic [3:0] in1, // 4-bit input 1
    input logic [3:0] in2, // 4-bit input 2
    input logic [3:0] in3, // 4-bit input 3
    input logic [1:0] sel, // 2-bit selection signal
    output logic [3:0] out // 4-bit output
);
    // Nested conditional operator 
    // C = (A > B) ? 1 : (A < B) ? 0 : 1 
    assign out = (sel == 2'b00) ? in0 :
                 (sel == 2'b01) ? in1 :
                 (sel == 2'b10) ? in2 :
                 (sel == 2'b11) ? in3 :
                 4'b0000; // Default case 

endmodule

2.4.2.1 Explanation

Module Declaration: The module mux4to1 is declared with inputs and outputs.
Inputs: Four 4-bit inputs (in0, in1, in2, in3) and a 2-bit selection signal (sel).
Output: One 4-bit output (out).
Conditional Statement: The assign statement uses a series of conditional (ternary) operators to select one of the four inputs based on the value of the 2-bit selection signal (sel).




2.4.3 4-bit adder
The 4-bit adder adds two 4-bit binary numbers and produces a 4-bit sum and a carry-out bit.
module adder4bit (
    input logic [3:0] a, // 4-bit input a
    input logic [3:0] b, // 4-bit input b
    output logic [3:0] sum, // 4-bit sum output
    output logic carry_out // Carry-out bit
);

    logic c1, c2, c3; // Intermediate carry bits

    // Half Adder for the least significant bit
    assign sum[0] = a[0] ^ b[0];
    assign c1 = a[0] & b[0];

    // Full Adder for the second bit
    assign sum[1] = a[1] ^ b[1] ^ c1;
    assign c2 = (a[1] & b[1]) | (c1 & (a[1] ^ b[1]));

    // Full Adder for the third bit
    assign sum[2] = a[2] ^ b[2] ^ c2;
    assign c3 = (a[2] & b[2]) | (c2 & (a[2] ^ b[2]));

    // Full Adder for the most significant bit
    assign sum[3] = a[3] ^ b[3] ^ c3;
    assign carry_out = (a[3] & b[3]) | (c3 & (a[3] ^ b[3]));

endmodule

2.4.3.1 Explanation

Module Declaration: The module adder4bit is declared with two 4-bit inputs (a and b), a 4-bit output (sum), and a carry-out bit (carry_out).
Intermediate Carry Bits: Three intermediate carry bits (c1, c2, c3) are used to store the carry from each adder stage.
Half Adder: The least significant bit is added using a half adder, which produces the sum and the first carry bit (c1).
Full Adders: The next three bits are added using full adders, which take into account the carry from the previous stage.
Final Carry-Out: The carry-out from the most significant bit is assigned to carry_out.




2.4.4 User Constraints Files and Pin Planning in Vivado
In Vivado, User Constraints Files (UCF) or Xilinx Design Constraints (XDC) files are used to define the physical constraints of the design, such as pin assignments, timing constraints, and other implementation-specific parameters. Pin planning involves mapping the logical signals in your design to the physical pins on the FPGA. This process ensures that the design interfaces correctly with external components and meets the required performance criteria. Proper pin planning and constraint management are crucial for successful FPGA implementation, as they directly impact signal integrity, timing closure, and overall design functionality.
The XDC file for Nexys A7 defines the pin placement for external signals of modules. To map the inputs of our adder4bit to the switches and the outputs to LEDs, we need to make the following changes:
##Switches
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN J15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { a[0] }]; #IO_L24N_T3_RS0_15 Sch=sw[0]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN L16   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { a[1] }]; #IO_L3N_T0_DQS_EMCCLK_14 Sch=sw[1]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN M13   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { a[2] }]; #IO_L6N_T0_D08_VREF_14 Sch=sw[2]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN R15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { a[3] }]; #IO_L13N_T2_MRCC_14 Sch=sw[3]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN R17   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { b[0] }]; #IO_L12N_T1_MRCC_14 Sch=sw[4]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN T18   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { b[1] }]; #IO_L7N_T1_D10_14 Sch=sw[5]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN U18   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { b[2] }]; #IO_L17N_T2_A13_D29_14 Sch=sw[6]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN R13   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { b[3] }]; #IO_L5N_T0_D07_14 Sch=sw[7]

##LEDS
## LEDs
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN H17   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { sum[0] }]; #IO_L18P_T2_A24_15 Sch=led[0]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN K15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { sum[1] }]; #IO_L24P_T3_RS1_15 Sch=led[1]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN J13   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { sum[2] }]; #IO_L17N_T2_A25_15 Sch=led[2]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN N14   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { sum[3] }]; #IO_L8P_T1_D11_14 Sch=led[3]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN R18   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { carry_out }]; #IO_L7P_T1_D09_14 Sch=led[4]
It is important to assign the appropriate pin to the get_ports function.

title: 2  Second exercise: Introduction to (System)Verilog
text:
2.5 Assignment
Your task is to implement a “dummy” 4-bit Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) with the following interface: - a, b: 4-bit inputs - alu_control: 3-bit input for selecting the operation - c: 4-bit output



alu_control Value
Operation




000
Addition


001
Subtraction


010
Bitwise AND


011
Bitwise OR


100
Bitwise XOR


101
Compare (equal)


110
Pass-through b


111
Pass-through a









Note



The ALU is 4-bit rather than 6-bit specifically to keep addition/subtraction small. The open-source Artix-7 flow (F4PGA: Yosys + VPR) that Anvil uses has known weak spots mapping inferred carry-chain arithmetic (+/-) — the same CARRY4 logic behind the adder4bit example above — and wider inferred adders can blow up synthesis time and resource usage. Staying at 4 bits, matching adder4bit’s width, keeps you well clear of that.


Tips: 1. Employ operators and intermediate signals to obtain the results of each operation. 2. Connect input signals to the rightmost switches (SW0 to SW7), and selection signals to the leftmost switches (SW13 to SW15). The output signal should be connected to LEDs (LED0 to LED3). 3. Employ nested conditionals.

title: 3  Third exercise: Designing sequential circuits with SystemVerilog
text:
3.1 Designing D Flip-Flop in SystemVerilog
Vivado recognizes certain idioms and transforms them into specific sequential circuits. Other coding styles may simulate correctly but may synthesize into circuits with obvious or subtle errors. We will present the proper idioms to describe registers and latches.
The Verilog code for a D flip-flop (DFF) active on the positive clock edge with a synchronous reset is given below:
The always_ff has it roots from Verilog language. In Verilog we have always statement, written in form:
In the previous code, the statement is executed only when the event specified in the sensitivity list occurs. For the D-FF example, the event is posedge clk, meaning the statements inside always_ff will execute on the positive edge of the clock. Inside the always_ff block, we use an if/else statement for conditional operations. Notice that the non-blocking operator <= is used inside the always_ff block. On every positive edge of the clock, the block checks if the reset is active. If the reset is active, the output will be set to zero; otherwise, the input will be copied to the output. The always_ff construct behaves like the always construct but is specifically used to imply flip-flops and allows tools to produce a warning if anything else is implied.
Let us design 4-bit counter, which counts on positive edge and has active high reset
As in the previous example, every time posedge clk occurs, the counter will increment the value of the internal counter counter if reset is low. Otherwise, the counter will start counting from zero. Finally, we output the state of the internal counter to the output. Note that assign and always_ff work in parallel.

section: 3.4 Task: Implement a 4-bit Gray Code Counter
text:
3.4 Task: Implement a 4-bit Gray Code Counter
Your task is to implement a 4-bit Gray Code counter, that changes its state with the frequency of 1 Hz.
Steps required: 1. Start with two counters: a modulo 10010^6 counter and a classical binary counter that counts from 0 to 15. 2. The first counter increments its value every system clock cycle. 3. The other counter changes its value when the first counter reaches the value 10010^6-1. When the input up_down is equal to 0, the counter increments its value; otherwise it decreases. 4. Convert the state of the binary counter to Gray Code.
Python code snippet that illustrates the behaviour of gray code counter
binary_count = 0;

while(1):
    for i in range (0, 100 * 1e6): # the module 100*1e6 counter 
        if(i==100 * 1e6-1):
            if(up_down==0):
                binary_count = binary_count + 1
            else:
                binary_count = binary_count - 1
    
    gray_code = bin2gray(binary_count )
def bin2gray(binary):
    match binary:
        case 0: return 0
        case 1: return 1
        case 2: return 3
        case 3: return 2
        case 4: return 6
        case 5: return 7
        case 6: return 5
        case 7: return 4
        case 8: return 12
        case 9: return 13
        case 10: return 15
        case 11: return 14
        case 12: return 10
        case 13: return 11
        case 14: return 9
        case 15: return 8
        case _: return 0 

3.4.1 Example Code Structure:
module gray_code_counter (
    input logic clk, 
    input logic rst, // Button 
    input logic up_down, // Switch for up/down counting 
    output logic [3:0] gray_code // connect the output to LEDs 
);

    logic en;
    logic [3:0] binary_count;

    // Prescaler code & binary counter 


    // Gray Code Converter 
    // employ always_comb and case statement 
    // to convert from code to another 

endmodule

title: 3  Third exercise: Designing sequential circuits with SystemVerilog
text:
3.5 Implementation guidelines
Structural modeling, splitting a design into separate modules and instantiating them, is introduced in the next exercise. For now gray_code_counter stays a single module, so the three pieces below are not separate modules with their own ports, but three cooperating pieces of behavioral code inside gray_code_counter, sharing the internal signals en and binary_count already declared in the skeleton above. These three pieces of code are actually three separate always blocks, where first two are always_ff and the last one is always_comb. The first two blocks are sequential, the last one is combinational. The three pieces are described below.

3.5.1 Divider
The divider turns the 100 MHz system clock into a single, once-per-second pulse on en. It is a free running counter, the same idea you will meet again as the standalone prescaler module in the next exercise.
Declare an internal register wide enough to count up to 100,000,000:
logic [26:0] div_count; // 2^27 > 100,000,000
Behavior:

On every rising edge of clk, if rst is high, reset div_count to zero.
Otherwise, increment div_count by one on every rising edge. This is step 2 from above, the first counter incrementing every system clock cycle.
When div_count reaches 100,000,000 - 1, drive en high for that clock cycle and let div_count wrap back to zero on the next edge, restarting the count.
The result is a single clock cycle pulse on en once every 100,000,000 clock cycles. At 100 MHz that is exactly once per second.



3.5.2 Up/down binary counter
binary_count is the 4-bit counter whose value eventually gets Gray encoded for the LEDs. Unlike div_count, it does not advance on every clock edge. It only advances once per second, on a clock edge where en is high.
Behavior:

On every rising edge of clk, if rst is high, reset binary_count to zero.
Otherwise, only change binary_count on a clock edge where en is high. When up_down is 0, increment binary_count, wrapping from 15 back to 0. When up_down is 1, decrement it, wrapping from 0 back to 15.
On a clock edge where en is low, hold binary_count at its current value.
Because en pulses only once per second, binary_count also only changes once per second, which is where the counter’s 1 Hz update rate comes from.



3.5.3 Gray code converter
The converter has no state of its own. It is a purely combinational function of binary_count, mapping each of the 16 possible values to the corresponding Gray code word from the bin2gray table above.
Behavior:

Use always_comb with a case statement on binary_count, one branch per value 0 through 15, assigning the matching Gray code word to gray_code in each branch.
Always include a default branch, even though cases 0 through 15 already cover every possible 4-bit value. The Common mistakes section earlier in this chapter explains why an incomplete case without a default infers a latch instead of the combinational logic you intended.
Because the conversion is combinational, gray_code updates immediately whenever binary_count changes. No separate clocking is needed here. binary_count already only changes once per second, so gray_code will too.



3.5.4 Pin mapping
Connect the clk signal to the system clock (100 MHz), the rst signal to the middle button, the up_down signal to the switch, and the gray_code signal to the LEDs.
## Clock signal
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN E3    IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { clk }]; #IO_L12P_T1_MRCC_35 Sch=clk100mhz
create_clock -add -name sys_clk_pin -period 10.00 -waveform {0 5} [get_ports {clk}];


##Switches
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN J15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { up_down }]; #IO_L24N_T3_RS0_15 Sch=sw[0]

## LEDs
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN H17   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { gray_code[0] }]; #IO_L18P_T2_A24_15 Sch=led[0]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN K15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { gray_code[1] }]; #IO_L24P_T3_RS1_15 Sch=led[1]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN J13   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { gray_code[2] }]; #IO_L17N_T2_A25_15 Sch=led[2]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN N14   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { gray_code[3] }]; #IO_L8P_T1_D11_14 Sch=led[3]

##Buttons
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN N17   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { rst }]; #IO_L9P_T1_DQS_14 Sch=btnc

title: 4  Fourth exercise: Structural modeling and Simulation
text:
4.1 Parametrized components
In the previous exercise, we focused on designing counters or flip-flops by describing their functionality in SystemVerilog. This style of modeling is referred to as behavioral modeling. This exercise focuses on structural modeling, where we describe a module in terms of how it is composed of simpler modules. In the example below, we assemble a 4:1 multiplexer from three 2:1 multiplexers. Each copy of the 2:1 multiplexer is called an instance and has a unique name.
As we can see, the instantiation of a module has following syntax: first, we specify the module name, followed by the instance name. In parentheses, we connect the module’s inputs and outputs to signals defined at the current level of hierarchy.
The bellow image depicts the resulting design:
So far, all of our modules have had fixed-width inputs and outputs. SystemVerilog allows variable-width modules through the use of parameterized modules. The code below illustrates a parameterized counter module with a variable length output signal.
This module defines a counter with a parameterized width. To instatiate in a another module, we need to do following:
To define parameters inside a module, we can use local parameters (localparam). Verilog HDL local parameters are identical to parameters except that they cannot be directly modified by defparam statements or module instance parameter value assignments.

section: 4.3 Task: Implement a PWM (Pulse-Width Modulation) module for RGB LED
text:
4.3 Task: Implement a PWM (Pulse-Width Modulation) module for RGB LED
In this task, you will implement a PWM module for an RGB LED. The module will have three 6-bit inputs, each controlling the duty cycle of the red, green, and blue LEDs. The module will have three 1-bit outputs, each representing the PWM signal for the red, green, and blue LEDs.
The PWM signal will be generated by comparing the duty cycle with a 4-bit counter that increments with the PWM_tick signal. The PWM_tick signal is generated by a prescaler that outputs a pulse every 3125 clock cycles, corresponding to a frequency of 32 kHz. You will connect the PWM module to the prescaler and the RGB LED module according to the diagram below.


Note: The N16, R11, and G14 pins on the FPGA board are connected to the red, green, and blue LEDs of the RGB LED, respectively.

Switch values denote duty cycle for each color. The duty cycle is calculated as follows:



SW[1:0]
Duty_cycle




00
0 %


01
12.5 %


10
25 %


11
50 %



Duty cycle is definied as ratio of high signal to the period of the signal, e.g. 25% duty cycle means that the signal is high for 25% of the period.

4.3.1 PWM time diagram



4.3.2 Extension: oscilloscope probe
An LED only tells you the PWM signal’s average brightness. To actually see the waveform, duty cycle, and period on an oscilloscope, add two more switches, SW[7:6], that select which of the three RGB PWM signals gets mirrored onto a new single-bit output port, pwm_out. Wire pwm_out to a Pmod header pin so you can clip a scope probe onto it. For connecting the probe and reading the signal once it’s wired up, see the oscilloscope appendix.



SW[7:6]
pwm_out drives




00
RGB[0] (red)


01
RGB[1] (green)


10
RGB[2] (blue)


11
1'b0

title: 4  Fourth exercise: Structural modeling and Simulation
text:
4.4 Implementation guidelines

4.4.1 Prescaler
The prescaler turns the fast system clock into the slower pwm_tick the PWM module counts on. It is a free running counter that produces a single cycle pulse once every limit clock cycles. Its interface is already declared in the starter file:
module prescaler
    #(parameter PRESCALER_WIDTH = 8)
    (
        input logic clk,
        input logic rst,
        input logic [PRESCALER_WIDTH-1:0] limit,
        output logic pwm_tick
    );









Port
Direction
Width
Description




clk
input
1 bit
System clock. The counter advances on its rising edge.


rst
input
1 bit
Synchronous reset. Clears the internal counter while high.


limit
input
PRESCALER_WIDTH bits
Number of clock cycles between output pulses.


pwm_tick
output
1 bit
Pulses high for one clock cycle, once every limit cycles.



Behavior:

Keep an internal counter register. On every rising edge of clk, if rst is high, reset that counter to zero.
Otherwise, increment the counter by one on every rising edge.
When the counter reaches limit - 1, drive pwm_tick high for that clock cycle and let the counter wrap back to zero on the next edge, restarting the count.
The result is a periodic, single cycle pulse with a period of exactly limit clock cycles. With limit = 3125 and a 100 MHz clk, pwm_tick fires once every 31.25 microseconds, which is 32 kHz.



4.4.2 PWM controller
The PWM controller turns a 2-bit duty cycle selection into a single PWM output for one LED color. One instance drives the red LED, one drives green, one drives blue, each fed by its own pair of switches and all three sharing the same pwm_tick from the prescaler. Its interface is already declared in the starter file:
module PWM_controller
(
    input logic clk,
    input logic rst,
    input logic [1:0] SW,
    input logic pwm_tick,
    output logic PWM
);









Port
Direction
Width
Description




clk
input
1 bit
System clock, used to advance the internal counter register.


rst
input
1 bit
Synchronous reset. Clears the internal counter while high.


SW
input
2 bits
Duty cycle selector for this color, per the duty cycle table above.


pwm_tick
input
1 bit
One clock cycle pulse from the prescaler. Acts as a count enable.


PWM
output
1 bit
The pulse width modulated signal driving one RGB LED color.



Behavior:

Keep an internal 4-bit counter register. Unlike the prescaler, this counter does not advance on every clk edge. It advances by one only on a clk edge where pwm_tick is high, and wraps from 15 back to 0. Sixteen pwm_tick pulses therefore make up one full PWM period.
On a clk edge where rst is high, reset that counter to zero instead of counting.
Translate SW into a threshold on the same 0 to 15 scale as the counter, so it lines up with the duty cycle table: 00 maps to a threshold of 0, 01 to 2, 10 to 4, and 11 to 8 (0, 2, 4, and 8 sixteenths are 0%, 12.5%, 25%, and 50%).
Drive PWM combinationally from the comparison: high while the counter value is less than the threshold, low otherwise. Since the counter counts through all 16 values once per period, this produces a high pulse whose width, as a fraction of the period, equals the selected duty cycle.



4.4.3 Top level: rgb_controller
The top module has no logic of its own beyond the oscilloscope channel selector described below. It otherwise only wires the prescaler and three PWM_controller instances together, using structural modeling exactly as introduced at the start of this chapter. Its interface, extended with the oscilloscope probe from the task above, is already declared in the starter file:
module rgb_controller (
    input logic clock,
    input logic reset,
    input logic [7:0] SW,
    output logic [2:0] RGB,
    output logic pwm_out
);









Port
Direction
Width
Description




clock
input
1 bit
System clock (100 MHz), forwarded to every instance below.


reset
input
1 bit
Synchronous reset, forwarded to every instance below.


SW
input
8 bits
SW[5:0]: duty cycle selectors, two bits per color (SW[1:0] red, SW[3:2] green, SW[5:4] blue). SW[7:6]: oscilloscope channel select.


RGB
output
3 bits
One PWM signal per color: RGB[0] red, RGB[1] green, RGB[2] blue.


pwm_out
output
1 bit
Mirrors whichever RGB bit SW[7:6] selects, for probing with an oscilloscope.



Structure:

One instance of prescaler, driven by clock/reset and the limit_value already wired up in the draft, produces a single pwm_tick signal shared by everything downstream.
Three instances of PWM_controller, conventionally named PWM_red, PWM_green, and PWM_blue. These are three separate instances of the exact same module, the same way mux2to1 was instantiated three times to build mux4to1 earlier in this chapter, not three different modules. Each instance shares clock, reset, and the one pwm_tick from the prescaler, but connects to a different 2-bit slice of SW and drives a different bit of RGB. For example, the red instance looks like:

PWM_controller PWM_red (
    .clk(clock),
    .rst(reset),
    .SW(SW[1:0]),
    .pwm_tick(pwm_tick),
    .PWM(RGB[0])
);
PWM_green and PWM_blue follow the same pattern, connecting SW[3:2]/RGB[1] and SW[5:4]/RGB[2] respectively. The draft file’s instantiation comments all read “for the red LED”. That’s a leftover from copy-pasting the first instance, and should read green and blue for the other two.

On top of the three instances above, drive pwm_out from RGB with a combinational multiplexer on SW[7:6], using always_comb and case exactly as introduced for Mux4to1 in the previous exercise:

always_comb begin
    case (SW[7:6])
        2'b00: pwm_out = RGB[0];
        2'b01: pwm_out = RGB[1];
        2'b10: pwm_out = RGB[2];
        default: pwm_out = 1'b0;
    endcase
end
SW[7:6] = 2'b11 has no explicit case, so it falls through to default, holding pwm_out at 1'b0 rather than leaving it undriven. Always keep that default branch, even on cases that look fully covered. Leaving it out, as the “Infering latch” mistake earlier in the previous chapter explains, would infer a latch instead of the combinational multiplexer you want.

Create a testbench to verify the functionality of your PWM module. The testbench is provided in the repository.



4.4.4 Testbenches for prescaler and PWM_controller
Before wiring everything together, verify prescaler and PWM_controller on their own, the same way tb_mux4to1 and tb_counter tested individual modules earlier in this chapter. A bug isolated to one small module is far easier to find than the same bug hiding inside the fully assembled rgb_controller.

4.4.4.1 tb_prescaler
module tb_prescaler;

    // Testbench signals
    logic clk;
    logic rst;
    logic [7:0] limit;
    logic pwm_tick;

    // Instantiate the DUT
    prescaler dut (
        .clk(clk),
        .rst(rst),
        .limit(limit),
        .pwm_tick(pwm_tick)
    );

    // Clock generation
    always begin
        #5 clk = ~clk; // Toggle clock every 5 time units
    end

    // Test procedure
    initial begin
        $dumpfile("tb_prescaler.vcd");
        $dumpvars(0, tb_prescaler);

        clk = 0;
        rst = 1;
        limit = 5;
        #10;
        rst = 0;

        // Let the counter run through several periods
        #200;

        $finish;
    end

    // Log every pwm_tick pulse
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (pwm_tick)
            $display("t=%0t pwm_tick pulse", $time);
    end

endmodule






Note



Do not test with limit = 3125, the value you will eventually use on hardware. At 100 MHz that is a pulse every 31.25 microseconds, so watching even a handful of periods in simulation means sitting through thousands of clock cycles of $display output or a huge waveform. Drive limit with a small value instead, such as 5 as above, so pwm_tick fires every few clock cycles and you can see several full periods and the counter wraparound in a short simulation run. Once the counting and wraparound logic is confirmed correct at a small limit, the same logic is correct at limit = 3125, only slower.




4.4.4.2 tb_pwm_controller
PWM_controller takes pwm_tick as an input rather than generating it, so this testbench stands in for the prescaler with a small free running counter of its own, pulsing pwm_tick high for one clock cycle out of every 4, instead of instantiating a full prescaler with a large limit. The DUT’s internal counter then advances once every 4 clock cycles, so a full 16-step PWM period takes 64 clock cycles to simulate, still far shorter than testing against the real limit = 3125 prescaler.
module tb_pwm_controller;

    // Testbench signals
    logic clk;
    logic rst;
    logic [1:0] SW;
    logic pwm_tick;
    logic PWM;

    // Instantiate the DUT
    PWM_controller dut (
        .clk(clk),
        .rst(rst),
        .SW(SW),
        .pwm_tick(pwm_tick),
        .PWM(PWM)
    );

    // Clock generation
    always begin
        #5 clk = ~clk; // Toggle clock every 5 time units
    end

    // Stand in for the prescaler: pulse pwm_tick high for one cycle
    // out of every 4 clock cycles
    logic [1:0] tick_count;

    always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
        tick_count <= tick_count + 1;
    end

    assign pwm_tick = (tick_count == 2'd3);

    // Test procedure
    initial begin
        $dumpfile("tb_pwm_controller.vcd");
        $dumpvars(0, tb_pwm_controller);

        clk = 0;
        rst = 1;
        tick_count = 0;
        SW = 2'b00;
        #10;
        rst = 0;

        // Run two full 64-cycle periods (1280 time units) at each duty cycle
        SW = 2'b00; #1280;   // 0 %
        SW = 2'b01; #1280;   // 12.5 %
        SW = 2'b10; #1280;   // 25 %
        SW = 2'b11; #1280;   // 50 %

        $finish;
    end

    // Log every PWM transition, so you can measure how long it stays
    // high relative to the 16-cycle period for each SW value
    always @(PWM) begin
        $display("t=%0t SW=%b PWM=%b", $time, SW, PWM);
    end

endmodule
Both testbenches call $dumpfile/$dumpvars up front, so running them through anvil test or iverilog/vvp produces a .vcd file you can open with gtkwave tb_prescaler.vcd & or gtkwave tb_pwm_controller.vcd &, as described earlier in this chapter. Watching pwm_tick and the internal counters directly in the waveform is often faster than reading through $display output.



4.4.5 Pin mapping
Connect the clock signal to the system clock (100 MHz), the reset signal to the middle button, switches SW[5:0] to the duty-cycle inputs (two bits per color), switches SW[7:6] to the oscilloscope channel select, the three RGB[2:0] outputs to the RGB LED, and pwm_out to a Pmod header pin for the scope probe. Add these to the project’s .xdc file, following the same set_property PACKAGE_PIN / set_property IOSTANDARD pattern used in the tools intro:
## Clock signal
set_property PACKAGE_PIN E3 [get_ports {clock}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {clock}]
create_clock -period 10.0 [get_ports {clock}]

## Switches
set_property PACKAGE_PIN J15 [get_ports {SW[0]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {SW[0]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN L16 [get_ports {SW[1]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {SW[1]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN M13 [get_ports {SW[2]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {SW[2]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN R15 [get_ports {SW[3]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {SW[3]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN R17 [get_ports {SW[4]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {SW[4]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN T18 [get_ports {SW[5]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {SW[5]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN U18 [get_ports {SW[6]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {SW[6]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN R13 [get_ports {SW[7]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {SW[7]}]

## Buttons
set_property PACKAGE_PIN N17 [get_ports {reset}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {reset}]

## RGB LEDs
set_property PACKAGE_PIN R12 [get_ports {RGB[2]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {RGB[2]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN M16 [get_ports {RGB[1]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {RGB[1]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN N15 [get_ports {RGB[0]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {RGB[0]}]

## Pmod Header JA, oscilloscope probe
set_property PACKAGE_PIN C17 [get_ports {pwm_out}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {pwm_out}]

title: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator
text:
5.1 Equipment
This appendix covers the two pieces of lab equipment you will connect to the FPGA board whenever an exercise asks you to probe a signal directly, starting with the oscilloscope extension in the PWM RGB exercise. The same equipment and the same Pmod probing convention come back again in the SoC verification lab later in the course.
Simulation only shows how a design behaves in an idealized model. Real hardware adds effects simulation cannot show you: clock jitter, I/O delays, signal integrity issues, and interaction with external peripherals. Measurement equipment lets you check timing, frequency, and duty cycle against the actual signal coming off the board, not just the one your testbench predicts.
crumbs: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator

title: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator
text:
Oscilloscope: Rigol DHO914, a digital oscilloscope used to capture and analyze electrical signals in real time.
Signal generator: Rigol DG912 Pro, used wherever an exercise asks you to compare a signal from the board against a known reference waveform.








WarningPower-on order



Turn the equipment on in this order: oscilloscope first, then the signal generator, then the FPGA board. Powering them on in a different order risks damaging the equipment.
crumbs: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator

title: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator
section: 5.2 Connecting probes to the FPGA board
text:
5.2 Connecting probes to the FPGA board
Several exercises route the signal to observe out through the JA Pmod header, using pin 1 as the signal and pin 5 as ground. The pinout is:


Connect the oscilloscope probe’s ground clip to the GND pin (pin 5) of the JA Pmod header.
Connect the probe tip to the signal pin (pin 1) of the JA Pmod header, for example the pwm_out signal from the PWM RGB exercise.
Also connect the FPGA board’s ground to the oscilloscope’s ground, so both share a common reference point.


Set the probe’s attenuation switch to 1X. A 10X setting attenuates the signal before it reaches the oscilloscope and will distort your reading.

If an exercise also asks you to compare against a reference signal from the signal generator, connect the generator’s output (CH1) to the oscilloscope’s second channel (CH2) with a BNC cable.
crumbs: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator

title: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator
text:
5.3 Using the Rigol DHO914 oscilloscope
When you power on the oscilloscope, the main screen displays the waveforms captured on each channel.

The yellow box next to the RIGOL logo in the lower left corner shows which channel is currently selected, CH1 in the image above. Press a channel’s button on the front panel to select it. Each channel has its own vertical scale, coupling, and position settings.

5.3.1 Adjusting the display
The waveform grid’s horizontal axis is time, the vertical axis is voltage.


The Sec/DIV knob sets the time scale, how much time one horizontal grid division represents.
Each channel’s Volts/DIV knob sets that channel’s voltage scale, how much voltage one vertical grid division represents.
Each channel’s Position knob, and the Horizontal Position knob, move the waveform on screen without changing its scale. Use them to center a waveform for a closer look.
The Auto button automatically picks scale and position settings for whatever signal is connected. It’s a good starting point when you aren’t yet sure what the signal looks like.
The Run/Stop button freezes the current acquisition. Press it again to resume capturing.



5.3.2 Measuring signal parameters
Press the Measure button (or the Measure knob, to the left of the Auto button) to open the measurement menu.

Measurements are grouped into three categories:

Vertical: voltage-related measurements such as Vmax, Vmin, Vavg, Vpp, and Vrms.
Time: time-related measurements such as Frequency, Period, Rise Time, Fall Time, and Duty Cycle.
Other: delay, phase, and similar cross-channel measurements.

Select the parameters relevant to what you’re verifying. For a PWM signal that is usually Period, Freq, and +Duty.

Close the measurement menu once you’ve made your selections. The chosen measurements stay on screen on the right side of the waveform display and update live as the oscilloscope keeps capturing.
crumbs: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator

title: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator
section: 5.4 Using the DG912 Pro signal generator
text:
5.4 Using the DG912 Pro signal generator
The DG912 Pro outputs sine, square, triangle, pulse, noise, DC, and arbitrary waveforms through two channels, CH1 and CH2. Most exercises only need CH1.

For each channel you can set:


Waveform type: square, sine, triangle, ramp, pulse, noise, DC, or arbitrary.
Frequency: press FREQ, enter the value on the numeric keypad, and confirm with ENTER.
Amplitude: press VPP to set the peak-to-peak voltage, or OFFSET to set the DC offset the waveform is centered around. An offset of 0V means the waveform swings between +VPP/2 and -VPP/2. The Ampl/HighL button switches between VPP/offset and high/low voltage level entry, whichever is more convenient for the levels you need.
Duty cycle (square waves): press DUTY, enter a percentage from 0 to 100, and confirm with ENTER. Duty cycle is the fraction of one period the signal spends high. 50% means high for half the period and low for the other half.
Phase: press PHASE and enter a value in degrees from 0 to 360, the shift of the waveform relative to a reference point in time.

Once configured, enable the channel’s output by pressing the gray area next to it. It lights up yellow when the output is active.

To match a 3.3V FPGA output level on a reference channel, set VPP to 3.3V and Offset to 1.65V, so the signal swings from 0V to 3.3V instead of being centered on 0V.
crumbs: 5  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator
